q: The study of fluids at rest is called _____.
e: The study of fluids at rest is called hydrostatics, while the study of fluids in motion is hydrodynamic.

q: The study of fluids at motion is called _____.
e: Hydrodynamic is the study of fluids at motion, whereas hydrostatics is the study of fluids at rest.

q: Pressure is defined as the force exerted normally on _____.
e: Pressure is defined as the force exerted normally on unit area, expressed as $p = \frac{F}{A}$.

q: In SI units, pressure is measured in _____.
e: In SI units, pressure is measured in 'pascal' (Pa).

q: The relation between pascal, newton and metre is $1 \text{ Pa} =$ _____.
e: One pascal is equivalent to one newton per square metre ($1 \text{ Pa} = 1 \text{ N m}^{-2}$).

q: The force in the pressure formula must be _____ to the surface.
e: The force in the pressure formula must be normal ($90^{\circ}$) to the surface.

q: Pressure is a _____ quantity.
e: Pressure is a scalar quantity because it has magnitude but no specific direction.

q: Pointed nails penetrate the surfaces because for a definite force, the exerted area is too _____.
e: For a definite force, a smaller exerted area results in higher pressure, allowing pointed nails to penetrate surfaces.

q: Sharp knives can cut more easily than blunt knives because of _____ cutting area.
e: Sharp knives have a smaller cutting area, which increases the pressure exerted for the same force.

q: Elephants have four large flat feet so they _____ the pressure and are less likely to sink into the ground.
e: Large flat feet increase the area, which reduces the pressure exerted on the ground.

q: In the FPS system, the unit of pressure is _____.
e: In the FPS system, the unit of pressure is pound per square inch (psi).

q: In Meteorology, the unit of pressure is _____.
e: In Meteorology, the unit of pressure is commonly expressed as hectopascal (hPa).

q: Standard Atmospheric Pressure is _____ atmosphere (1 atm).
e: Standard Atmospheric Pressure is defined as 1 atmosphere (1 atm).

q: The relation $1 \text{ atm} = 1.013 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa} =$ _____ millimetre mercury.
e: Standard atmospheric pressure is equivalent to 760 millimetre mercury (760 mm Hg).

q: $1 \text{ atm} = 1013 \text{ hPa} =$ _____ millibar (mb).
e: One atmosphere is equal to 1013 hPa, which is also equal to 1013 millibar (mb).

q: $1 \text{ hPa} = 100 \text{ Pa} =$ _____ mb.
e: One hectopascal is equal to 100 pascals and exactly 1 millibar (mb).

q: $1 \text{ psi} =$ _____ Pa.
e: One pound per square inch (psi) is equivalent to $6.90 \times 10^3$ Pa.

q: Density is the ratio of _____ to volume of a substance.
e: Density is defined as the ratio of mass to volume of a substance.

q: Density is a _____ quantity.
e: Density is a scalar quantity as it only has magnitude and no direction.

q: In the density formula, $\rho$ represents a _____ alphabet.
e: The symbol $\rho$ (rho) used for density is a Greek alphabet letter.

q: In SI unit, density is expressed in _____.
e: In SI units, density is expressed in kilogram per cubic metre ($\text{kg m}^{-3}$).

q: In CGS unit, density is expressed in gram per cubic centimetre ($\text{g cm}^{-3}$) or _____.
e: In CGS units, density can also be expressed as gram per millilitre ($\text{g mL}^{-1}$).

q: Mass of an object can be measured using a _____.
e: The mass of an object is measured using a balance, while volume is measured using a measuring cylinder.

q: Volume of a substance can be measured using a _____.
e: Volume can be measured using a measuring cylinder.

q: Mass of the object does not change, but the volume depends on the _____.
e: While mass remains constant, the volume of a substance depends on its temperature.

q: If the volume changes, the _____ will change.
e: Since density is mass divided by volume, a change in volume will result in a change in density.

q: According to Table 4.1, the density of water at $4^{\circ}\text{C}$ is _____ $\text{kg m}^{-3}$.
e: The density of water at $4^{\circ}\text{C}$ is $1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ (or $1 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$).

q: According to Table 4.1, the density of mercury is _____ $\text{kg m}^{-3}$.
e: The density of mercury is listed as $13600 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$.

q: According to Table 4.1, the density of gold is _____ $\text{kg m}^{-3}$.
e: The density of gold is $19300 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$.

q: The average density of a human body is a little _____ than water density.
e: The average density of a human body is a little less than water density, which aids in floating.

q: Relative density is how much a substance is denser than _____.
e: Relative density is defined as how much a substance is denser than water.

q: Relative density is also known as _____.
e: Relative density is also commonly known as specific gravity.

q: The formula for relative density is the density of substance divided by the density of water at _____.
e: Relative density is calculated using the density of water at $4^{\circ}\text{C}$ as the reference.

q: As the density of water is $1 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$ in CGS units, the density of substance can be taken as the _____.
e: In CGS units, since water's density is $1 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$, the numerical value of the substance's density equals its relative density.

q: Relative density is just a number without _____.
e: Because it is the ratio of two densities, relative density is a unitless number.

q: Archimedes' Principle Part I states that an immersed object displaces liquid volume equal to the volume of the _____ portion.
e: Part I of Archimedes' Principle states the displaced liquid volume equals the volume of the immersed portion.

q: Archimedes' Principle Part II states that the loss in weight of the object is equal to the _____ of the liquid displaced.
e: Part II states that the loss in weight of the object equals the weight of the liquid displaced.

q: The upward thrust acting on a body immersed in a liquid is equal to the weight of the _____ displaced by the body.
e: Upward thrust is equal to the weight of the liquid displaced by the body.

q: Upward thrust is also known as uplift force or _____.
e: Upward thrust, uplift force, and buoyancy are synonymous terms in this context.

q: By Archimedes' principle, if the weight of a body is more than buoyancy, it will _____ in the liquid.
e: If the weight of a body exceeds the upward buoyant force, the body will sink.

q: Substances having relative density greater than _____ will sink in water.
e: Substances with a relative density greater than one are denser than water and will sink.

q: When an object is placed in a liquid of a lower density, the object _____.
e: An object will sink when placed in a liquid that has a lower density than the object itself.

q: If an object is placed in a liquid of a greater density, it _____.
e: An object will float if it is placed in a liquid of greater density.

q: The amount of submerged portion for a floating body is _____ proportional to the specific gravity of the liquid.
e: The submerged portion is inversely proportional to the specific gravity of the liquid.

q: The more submerged a floating body is, the _____ the specific gravity.
e: Because of the inverse proportionality, more submersion indicates a lower specific gravity of the liquid.

q: The hydrometer is an instrument for measuring the density (or) _____ of liquids.
e: A hydrometer is specifically designed to measure the density or relative density of liquids.

q: A hydrometer usually consists of a glass tube with a long _____ at one end.
e: The device typically features a glass tube with a long bulb at one end.

q: The bulb of a hydrometer is weighted with _____ so that the device floats vertically.
e: The bulb is weighted with lead shot to ensure the hydrometer floats vertically in the liquid.

q: The relative density of a liquid is read off the calibrated stem of a hydrometer by the _____.
e: The reading is taken from the calibrated stem based on the depth of immersion.

q: If the hydrometer floats higher, it indicates that the liquid has a _____ density.
e: Floating higher means less of the device is submerged, indicating a higher density liquid.

q: The hydrometer sinks in the liquid until the weight of the liquid displaced is equal to the _____ of the hydrometer.
e: It sinks until the buoyant force (weight of displaced liquid) equals the total weight of the hydrometer.

q: The hydrometer is calibrated to measure the density of the liquid in _____.
e: The hydrometer is calibrated to measure density in $\text{kg m}^{-3}$.

q: Special hydrometers are used to test the specific gravity of solutions in _____ in order to determine the condition of the battery.
e: Special hydrometers are used to test the acid in storage batteries to determine their condition.

q: The relative density of the acid in a fully charged car battery is _____.
e: The relative density of the acid in a fully charged car battery is 1.25.

q: Milk and wine can be tested with a hydrometer to make sure they have not been diluted with _____.
e: Hydrometers are used to check if milk and wine have been adulterated or diluted with water.

q: A test tube used as a hydrometer must have an overall density less than one or less than the density of _____.
e: To function as a hydrometer, the test tube must have an overall density less than that of water so it can float.

q: Force exerted on a sail in a low pressure area is due to the atmospheric pressure _____.
e: As noted in the textbook hints, force exerts due to the atmospheric pressure difference.

q: In the Archimedes crown problem, the added metal was suspected to be copper because it has a similar _____ to gold.
e: The textbook hints that copper was the likely added metal because it has a similar color to gold.

q: The density of pure gold is _____ $\text{g cm}^{-3}$.
e: The density of gold is stated as $19.3 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$ in the Archimedes crown example.

q: In the crown problem, Archimedes found the actual volume of the crown to be _____ $\text{cm}^3$.
e: Archimedes found the volume of the crown to be $315 \text{ cm}^3$, proving it was not pure gold.

q: The mass of the King's crown in the Archimedes problem was _____ g.
e: The crown had a mass of 3.75 kg, which is equivalent to 3750 g.

q: For a floating hydrometer, the weight of the hydrometer equals the volume of liquid displaced multiplied by the density of the liquid and _____.
e: The formula is $\text{Weight} = (\text{volume displaced} \times \text{density}) \times g$.
